questions.q:
Which of the following is correct in the case of the Bohr model of atoms?
A. Predicts continuous emission spectra for all atoms
B. Assumes that the angular momentum of electrons is quantised
C. Predicts same emission spectrum for singly ionised neon atom and hydrogen atom
D. Predicts same emission spectrum for singly ionised neon atom and singly ionised helium atom
questions.solution:
The Bohr model of the atom is based on several postulates, one of which is the quantization of angular momentum. According to this postulate, the angular momentum $L$ of an electron revolving in a stable orbit is an integral multiple of $\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$, expressed as $L = n\dfrac{h}{2\pi}$, where $n$ is an integer.

Regarding the other options: The Bohr model predicts line spectra, not continuous spectra, for hydrogen-like atoms. The emission spectrum depends on the atomic number $Z$, as the energy levels are given by $E_n = -13.6 \dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}$ eV. Since hydrogen ($Z=1$) and singly ionised neon ($Z=10$) have different atomic numbers, their emission spectra are different. Similarly, singly ionised neon ($Z=10$) and singly ionised helium ($Z=2$) have different atomic numbers and thus different spectra.

Answer: B

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A capacitor of capacitance $4 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ is charged to a potential of 24 V and then connected in parallel to an uncharged capacitor of capacitance $6 \mu \mathrm{~F}$. The final potential difference across each capacitor will be:
questions.solution:
The initial charge $Q$ on the capacitor of capacitance $C_1 = 4 \mu \text{F}$ charged to a potential $V_1 = 24 \text{V}$ is given by $Q = C_1 V_1$.

$Q = 4 \mu \text{F} \times 24 \text{V} = 96 \mu \text{C}$.

When this capacitor is connected in parallel to an uncharged capacitor of capacitance $C_2 = 6 \mu \text{F}$, the total charge $Q$ is redistributed between the two capacitors until they reach a common potential $V$.

The total capacitance of the parallel combination is $C_{eq} = C_1 + C_2 = 4 \mu \text{F} + 6 \mu \text{F} = 10 \mu \text{F}$.

Using the principle of conservation of charge, $Q = C_{eq} V$.

$96 \mu \text{C} = 10 \mu \text{F} \times V$.

$V = \dfrac{96 \mu \text{C}}{10 \mu \text{F}} = 9.6 \text{V}$.

Answer: 9.6 V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A network of capacitors is as shown below. If the voltage supply is 100 V , find the energy stored in the $6 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ capacitor.
$C_1=3 \mu F, C_2=6 \mu F, C_3=3 \mu F$ and $C_4=4 \mu F$
questions.solution:
The circuit consists of a capacitor $C_4$ in parallel with the series combination of $C_1, C_2,$ and $C_3$.

First, calculate the equivalent capacitance of the series branch containing $C_1, C_2,$ and $C_3$. Let this be $C_{series}$.

$\dfrac{1}{C_{series}} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} + \dfrac{1}{C_3} = \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2+1+2}{6} = \dfrac{5}{6} \mu F^{-1}$

$C_{series} = \dfrac{6}{5} = 1.2 \mu F$

The voltage across the series branch is equal to the supply voltage $V = 100 V$.

The charge $Q$ on the series branch is $Q = C_{series} \times V = 1.2 \mu F \times 100 V = 120 \mu C$.

Since $C_1, C_2,$ and $C_3$ are in series, they all carry the same charge $Q = 120 \mu C$.

The energy stored in the $C_2 = 6 \mu F$ capacitor is given by $U = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C_2}$.

$U = \dfrac{(120 \times 10^{-6})^2}{2 \times 6 \times 10^{-6}} = \dfrac{14400 \times 10^{-12}}{12 \times 10^{-6}} = 1200 \times 10^{-6} J = 1.2 \times 10^{-3} J = 1.2 mJ$.

Answer: 1.2 mJ

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Select the correct statement from the following: The position of the centre of mass of a system:
options: Does not depend on the shape and size of the system
Depend on the choice of coordinates
Depends on the distribution of its mass.
Remains the same in any translatory motion
questions.solution:
The position of the centre of mass of a system of particles is defined by the vector $\vec{R}_{cm} = \dfrac{\sum m_i \vec{r}_i}{\sum m_i}$.

This definition shows that the location of the centre of mass is determined by the individual masses $m_i$ and their respective position vectors $\vec{r}_i$ relative to the chosen origin.

Since the position vectors $\vec{r}_i$ depend on the distribution of mass within the system, the centre of mass is fundamentally a property of the mass distribution of the body or system.

While the numerical coordinates of the centre of mass change if the origin of the coordinate system is shifted, the physical location of the centre of mass relative to the body itself is fixed by the mass distribution, making the statement regarding mass distribution the most fundamental physical description.

Answer: Depends on the distribution of its mass.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: The velocity - mass graph of body with constant linear momentum is represented by the graph:
questions.solution:
Linear momentum $p$ is defined as the product of mass $m$ and velocity $v$, given by the equation $p = mv$.

For a body with constant linear momentum, $p$ is a constant. Therefore, we can write the relationship between velocity and mass as $v = \dfrac{p}{m}$.

This equation represents an inverse proportionality between velocity and mass, which is of the form $v \propto \dfrac{1}{m}$.

The graph of $v$ versus $m$ for this relationship is a rectangular hyperbola, where $v$ decreases as $m$ increases, approaching zero as $m$ approaches infinity, and approaching infinity as $m$ approaches zero.

Answer:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.chapter: Center of Mass, Momentum and Collision
questions.q: Momentum of a body is increased to three times its original value. By what percentage will its kinetic energy change?
questions.solution:
The kinetic energy $K$ of a body is related to its momentum $p$ by the formula $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, where $m$ is the mass of the body.

Let the initial momentum be $p_1 = p$ and the initial kinetic energy be $K_1 = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$.

The momentum is increased to three times its original value, so the new momentum is $p_2 = 3p$.

The new kinetic energy $K_2$ is given by $K_2 = \dfrac{p_2^2}{2m} = \dfrac{(3p)^2}{2m} = \dfrac{9p^2}{2m} = 9K_1$.

The change in kinetic energy is $\Delta K = K_2 - K_1 = 9K_1 - K_1 = 8K_1$.

The percentage change in kinetic energy is $\dfrac{\Delta K}{K_1} \times 100\% = \dfrac{8K_1}{K_1} \times 100\% = 800\%$.

Answer: $800 \%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The resistance of a heating element is found to be $120 \Omega$ at room temperature which is $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If the temperature coefficient of the material of the resistor is $1.6 \times 10^{-4} C^{-1}$ and the resistance is found to be $160 \Omega$, the temperature of the element is:
questions.solution:
The resistance of a conductor at a temperature $T$ is given by the formula $R_T = R_0 [1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]$, where $R_0$ is the resistance at room temperature $T_0$, $R_T$ is the resistance at temperature $T$, and $\alpha$ is the temperature coefficient of resistance.

Given values are $R_0 = 120 \Omega$, $T_0 = 20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, $R_T = 160 \Omega$, and $\alpha = 1.6 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{C}^{-1}$.

Substituting these values into the equation:

$160 = 120 [1 + 1.6 \times 10^{-4} (T - 20)]$

Dividing both sides by $120$:

$\dfrac{160}{120} = 1 + 1.6 \times 10^{-4} (T - 20)$

$\dfrac{4}{3} = 1 + 1.6 \times 10^{-4} (T - 20)$

$\dfrac{4}{3} - 1 = 1.6 \times 10^{-4} (T - 20)$

$\dfrac{1}{3} = 1.6 \times 10^{-4} (T - 20)$

$T - 20 = \dfrac{1}{3 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-4}}$

$T - 20 = \dfrac{1}{4.8 \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{10000}{4.8} \approx 2083.33$

$T = 2083.33 + 20 = 2103.33 \approx 2103^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

Answer: $2103^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The power dissipated across the $16 \Omega$ resistor in the circuit is 2 watts. The power dissipated in watt units across the $4 \Omega$ resistor is:
questions.solution:
The circuit consists of two parallel branches. The top branch contains a $16 \Omega$ resistor. The bottom branch contains a $6 \Omega$ resistor and a $4 \Omega$ resistor in series.

Let $V$ be the potential difference across the parallel branches. The power dissipated in the $16 \Omega$ resistor is given by $P_{16} = \dfrac{V^2}{R_{16}} = 2$ W. Substituting $R_{16} = 16 \Omega$, we get $\dfrac{V^2}{16} = 2$, which implies $V^2 = 32$ V$^2$.

The bottom branch has a total resistance $R_{bottom} = 6 \Omega + 4 \Omega = 10 \Omega$. The current flowing through the bottom branch is $I_{bottom} = \dfrac{V}{R_{bottom}} = \dfrac{V}{10}$.

The power dissipated in the $4 \Omega$ resistor is $P_4 = I_{bottom}^2 \times R_4 = \left(\dfrac{V}{10}\right)^2 \times 4 = \dfrac{V^2}{100} \times 4$.

Substituting $V^2 = 32$, we get $P_4 = \dfrac{32}{100} \times 4 = \dfrac{128}{100} = 1.28$ W.

Answer: 1.28 W

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A galvanometer having a resistance of $50 \Omega$ is shunted by a wire of resistance $10 \Omega$. If the total current is 2 A , the current passing through the shunt is:
questions.solution:
Let $G$ be the resistance of the galvanometer and $S$ be the resistance of the shunt wire. Given $G = 50 \Omega$ and $S = 10 \Omega$. The total current $I = 2 \text{ A}$.

The current $I_S$ passing through the shunt is given by the current divider rule:

$I_S = I \times \dfrac{G}{G + S}$

Substituting the given values:

$I_S = 2 \times \dfrac{50}{50 + 10}$

$I_S = 2 \times \dfrac{50}{60}$

$I_S = 2 \times \dfrac{5}{6}$

$I_S = \dfrac{5}{3} \text{ A}$

Answer: $\dfrac{5}{3} \mathrm{~A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A student measures the terminal potential difference $V$ of a cell of $\operatorname{emf} \varepsilon$ and internal resistance $r$ as a function of the current I flowing through it. Which of the following graphs will give the values of emf $\varepsilon$ and internal resistance $r$ ?
questions.solution:
The terminal potential difference $V$ of a cell with emf $\varepsilon$ and internal resistance $r$ is given by the equation $V = \varepsilon - Ir$.

This equation represents a linear relationship between $V$ and $I$, which can be written in the form $y = mx + c$ as $V = -rI + \varepsilon$.

Comparing this with the equation of a straight line, the intercept on the $V$-axis (when $I = 0$) is $\varepsilon$, and the slope of the line is $-r$.

Graph 1 shows $V$ on the vertical axis and $I$ on the horizontal axis with a negative slope, which matches the equation $V = -rI + \varepsilon$. The $V$-intercept is $\varepsilon$ and the magnitude of the slope gives the internal resistance $r$.

Answer: $1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The net resistance between the points A and B in the circuit given below is:
questions.solution:
A and E are the same node. The circuit forms a Wheatstone bridge with D and C as middle junctions.

Arms: $R_{ED} = 4R$, $R_{EC} = 2R$, $R_{DB} = 4R$, $R_{CB} = 2R$, cross resistor $= 5R$

Balance check: $\dfrac{R_{ED}}{R_{EC}} = \dfrac{4R}{2R} = 2$ and $\dfrac{R_{DB}}{R_{CB}} = \dfrac{4R}{2R} = 2$

Bridge is balanced \Rightarrow no current through $5R$, so it is removed.

Upper branch (E-D-B): $4R + 4R = 8R$
Lower branch (E-C-B): $2R + 2R = 4R$

$\dfrac{1}{R_{AB}} = \dfrac{1}{8R} + \dfrac{1}{4R} = \dfrac{3}{8R}$

$R_{AB} = \dfrac{8R}{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A plot of kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons from a metal versus the frequency of incident radiation gives a straight line, the intercept of which
A. Depends on the nature of the metal used
B. Depends on the intensity of radiation
C. Depends both on the intensity and the nature of metal used
D. Is a constant and is same for all metals which is independent of the intensity of Incident radiation
questions.solution:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the kinetic energy $K_{max}$ of emitted photoelectrons is given by $K_{max} = h u - \Phi$, where $h$ is Planck's constant, $ u$ is the frequency of incident radiation, and $\Phi$ is the work function of the metal.

The equation $K_{max} = h u - \Phi$ represents a straight line of the form $y = mx + c$, where $y = K_{max}$, $x = u$, $m = h$ (slope), and $c = -\Phi$ (intercept).

The intercept on the $y$-axis is $-\Phi$, which is the negative of the work function of the metal. Since the work function $\Phi$ is a characteristic property of the metal, the intercept depends solely on the nature of the metal used.

The intercept is independent of the intensity of the incident radiation, as intensity only affects the number of photoelectrons emitted, not their maximum kinetic energy.

Answer: A

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The stopping potential when a metal surface is illuminated by light of wavelength $\lambda$ is 15 V . The stopping potential when the same surface is illuminated by light of wavelength $4 \lambda$ is 3 V . The ratio of threshold wavelength to the initial incident wavelength $\lambda$ is:
questions.solution:
From Einstein's photoelectric equation, the stopping potential $V_s$ is given by $eV_s = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \Phi$, where $\Phi$ is the work function of the metal and $\lambda_0$ is the threshold wavelength such that $\Phi = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0}$.

For the first case, $eV_1 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = 15e$. Thus, $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = 15e$ (Equation 1).

For the second case, $eV_2 = \dfrac{hc}{4\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = 3e$. Thus, $\dfrac{hc}{4\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = 3e$ (Equation 2).

Subtracting Equation 2 from Equation 1:

$\left( \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{4\lambda} \right) = 15e - 3e = 12e$

$\dfrac{3hc}{4\lambda} = 12e \Rightarrow \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = 16e$.

Substituting $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = 16e$ into Equation 1:

$16e - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = 15e \Rightarrow \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = e$.

Since $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = 16e$ and $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} = e$, we have $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = 16 \left( \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0} \right)$, which implies $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{16}{\lambda_0}$.

Therefore, $\dfrac{\lambda_0}{\lambda} = 16$, or the ratio of threshold wavelength to the initial wavelength is $16:1$.

Answer: $16: 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rectangular coil of 250 turns has an average area of $20 \mathrm{~cm} \times 15 \mathrm{~cm}$. The coil rotates with a speed of 60 cycles per second in a uniform magnetic field of $2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~T}$ about an axis perpendicular to the field. The peak value of the induced emf is:
questions.solution:
The peak value of the induced electromotive force (emf) in a rotating coil is given by the formula $\varepsilon_{0} = N A B \omega$, where $N$ is the number of turns, $A$ is the area of the coil, $B$ is the magnetic field strength, and $\omega$ is the angular velocity.

Given values:
$N = 250$
$A = 20 \text{ cm} \times 15 \text{ cm} = 0.2 \text{ m} \times 0.15 \text{ m} = 0.03 \text{ m}^{2}$
$B = 2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ T}$
Frequency $f = 60 \text{ Hz}$
Angular velocity $\omega = 2 \pi f = 2 \pi \times 60 = 120 \pi \text{ rad/s}$

Substituting these values into the formula:
$\varepsilon_{0} = 250 \times 0.03 \times (2 \times 10^{-2}) \times 120 \pi$

Calculating the product:
$\varepsilon_{0} = 250 \times 0.03 \times 0.02 \times 120 \pi$
$\varepsilon_{0} = 7.5 \times 0.02 \times 120 \pi$
$\varepsilon_{0} = 0.15 \times 120 \pi$
$\varepsilon_{0} = 18 \pi \text{ volt}$

Answer: $18 \pi$ volt

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A plane electromagnetic wave with frequency 40 MHz travels in free space. At a particular point in space and time, the magnetic field is $2 \times 10^{-8} T$. What will be the electric field at this point?
questions.solution:
The relationship between the magnitude of the electric field $E$ and the magnetic field $B$ in an electromagnetic wave traveling in free space is given by $E = cB$, where $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum.

The speed of light in vacuum is $c = 3 \times 10^{8} \text{ m/s}$.

Given $B = 2 \times 10^{-8} \text{ T}$, we substitute the values into the equation:

$E = (3 \times 10^{8} \text{ m/s}) \times (2 \times 10^{-8} \text{ T})$

$E = 6 \times 10^{8-8} \text{ V/m}$

$E = 6 \times 10^{0} \text{ V/m} = 6 \text{ V/m}$.

Answer: $6 \mathrm{Vm}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bob of a simple pendulum has a mass of 4 g and a charge of $20 \mu \mathrm{C}$. If it is at rest in a uniform horizontal electric field of intensity $1000 \mathrm{Vm}^{-1}$, the angle that the pendulum makes with the vertical at equilibrium is:
questions.solution:
The forces acting on the bob at equilibrium are the gravitational force $mg$ acting vertically downwards, the electric force $qE$ acting horizontally, and the tension $T$ in the string.

Let $\theta$ be the angle the string makes with the vertical. At equilibrium, the forces balance as follows:

$T \sin \theta = qE$
$T \cos \theta = mg$

Dividing the two equations, we get:

$\tan \theta = \dfrac{qE}{mg}$

Given values are $m = 4 \text{ g} = 4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}$, $q = 20 \mu \text{C} = 20 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$, $E = 1000 \text{ Vm}^{-1}$, and taking $g = 10 \text{ ms}^{-2}$:

$\tan \theta = \dfrac{(20 \times 10^{-6}) \times 1000}{4 \times 10^{-3} \times 10}$

$\tan \theta = \dfrac{20 \times 10^{-3}}{40 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{20}{40} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Therefore, $\theta = \tan^{-1} \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)$.

Answer: $\tan ^{-1} \dfrac{1}{2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle of mass 3 g and charge $60 \mu \mathrm{C}$ is released from rest in a uniform electric field of intensity $10^5 N C^{-1}$. If the value of kinetic energy attained by the particle after moving through a distance of 2 cm is $m \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~J}$, then the value of m is:
questions.solution:
Given mass $m = 3 \text{ g} = 3 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg}$, charge $q = 60 \mu \text{C} = 60 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$, electric field $E = 10^5 \text{ N C}^{-1}$, and distance $d = 2 \text{ cm} = 0.02 \text{ m}$.

The force acting on the particle is $F = qE = (60 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}) \times (10^5 \text{ N C}^{-1}) = 6 \text{ N}$.

The work done by the electric field on the particle is $W = F \times d = 6 \text{ N} \times 0.02 \text{ m} = 0.12 \text{ J}$.

According to the work-energy theorem, the kinetic energy attained by the particle starting from rest is equal to the work done by the electric field.

Kinetic Energy $K = 0.12 \text{ J} = 12 \times 10^{-2} \text{ J}$.

Comparing this with the given expression $m \times 10^{-2} \text{ J}$, we find $m = 12$.

Answer: $12$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two electric dipoles of dipole moments $3.9 \times 10^{-30} \mathrm{Cm}$ and $5.2 \times 10^{-30} \mathrm{Cm}$ are placed in two different uniform electric fields of strengths $16 \times 10^4 N C^{-1}$ and $4 \times 10^4 N C^{-1}$ respectively. What is the ratio of maximum torque experienced by the electric dipoles?
questions.solution:
The torque $\tau$ experienced by an electric dipole of moment $p$ in a uniform electric field $E$ is given by $\tau = pE \sin \theta$.

The maximum torque $\tau_{max}$ occurs when $\theta = 90^{\circ}$, so $\tau_{max} = pE$.

For the first dipole, $p_1 = 3.9 \times 10^{-30} \text{ Cm}$ and $E_1 = 16 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$.
$\tau_{max,1} = (3.9 \times 10^{-30}) \times (16 \times 10^4) = 62.4 \times 10^{-26} \text{ Nm}$.

For the second dipole, $p_2 = 5.2 \times 10^{-30} \text{ Cm}$ and $E_2 = 4 \times 10^4 \text{ N C}^{-1}$.
$\tau_{max,2} = (5.2 \times 10^{-30}) \times (4 \times 10^4) = 20.8 \times 10^{-26} \text{ Nm}$.

The ratio of the maximum torques is $\dfrac{\tau_{max,1}}{\tau_{max,2}} = \dfrac{62.4 \times 10^{-26}}{20.8 \times 10^{-26}} = \dfrac{62.4}{20.8} = 3$.

Therefore, the ratio is $3:1$.

Answer: $3: 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three charges, $\mathrm{Q},-\mathrm{q}$ and 2 q are placed at the vertices of a right-angled isosceles triangle. What is the value of $q$ for the net electrostatic energy of the configuration to be zero?
questions.solution:
The electrostatic potential energy $U$ of a system of point charges is given by the sum of the potential energies of all pairs of charges: $U = \sum \dfrac{k q_i q_j}{r_{ij}}$.

The charges are $Q$, $2q$, and $-q$. The distances between the pairs are $r$, $r$, and $r\sqrt{2}$ (hypotenuse of the right-angled isosceles triangle).

The total potential energy $U$ is:
$U = \dfrac{k(Q)(2q)}{r} + \dfrac{k(Q)(-q)}{r\sqrt{2}} + \dfrac{k(2q)(-q)}{r} = 0$

Dividing by $\dfrac{kq}{r}$ (assuming $k, q, r \neq 0$):
$2Q - \dfrac{Q}{\sqrt{2}} - 2q = 0$

$2q = 2Q - \dfrac{Q}{\sqrt{2}}$

$2q = Q \left( 2 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right)$

$q = Q \left( 1 - \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} \right)$

Answer: $Q\left[1-\dfrac{1}{2 \sqrt{2}}\right]$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniformly charged conducting sphere of 0.2 m diameter has a surface charge density of $70 \mu \mathrm{Cm}^{-2}$. The electric flux leaving the surface of the sphere is:
questions.solution:
The diameter of the sphere is $d = 0.2$ m, so the radius is $r = 0.1$ m.

The surface area of the sphere is $A = 4 \pi r^2 = 4 \pi (0.1)^2 = 0.04 \pi$ m$^2$.

The total charge $Q$ on the sphere is given by $Q = \sigma A$, where $\sigma = 70 \times 10^{-6}$ C m$^{-2}$.

$Q = 70 \times 10^{-6} \times 0.04 \pi = 2.8 \pi \times 10^{-6}$ C.

According to Gauss's Law, the electric flux $\Phi$ leaving the surface is $\Phi = \dfrac{Q}{\epsilon_0}$.

Using $\epsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-12}$ C$^2$ N$^{-1}$ m$^{-2}$:

$\Phi = \dfrac{2.8 \pi \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} = \dfrac{2.8 \times 3.14159 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} \approx \dfrac{8.796 \times 10^{-6}}{8.854 \times 10^{-12}} \approx 0.993 \times 10^6$ N C$^{-1}$ m$^2$.

Rounding to the nearest value, $\Phi \approx 9.9 \times 10^5$ N C$^{-1}$ m$^2$.

Answer: $9.9 \times 10^5 N C^{-1} m^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
If the distance between the Sun and Earth is doubled ,then the duration of the year on earth will be:
[Given actual duration of the year $=\mathrm{T}$ ]
questions.solution:
According to Kepler's third law of planetary motion, the square of the time period $T$ of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis $r$ of its orbit, which is given by $T^2 \propto r^3$.

Let the initial distance be $r_1 = r$ and the initial time period be $T_1 = T$. The new distance is $r_2 = 2r$.

Using the relation $\dfrac{T_2^2}{T_1^2} = \left( \dfrac{r_2}{r_1} \right)^3$, we substitute the values:

$\dfrac{T_2^2}{T^2} = \left( \dfrac{2r}{r} \right)^3 = 2^3 = 8$.

Taking the square root on both sides, we get $\dfrac{T_2}{T} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$.

Therefore, the new duration of the year is $T_2 = 2\sqrt{2}T$.

Answer: $2 \sqrt{2} T$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The unit of universal gravitational constant is :
questions.solution:
The law of universal gravitation is given by the formula $F = G \dfrac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$, where $F$ is the gravitational force, $G$ is the universal gravitational constant, $m_1$ and $m_2$ are the masses of the two objects, and $r$ is the distance between them.

Rearranging the formula to solve for $G$, we get $G = \dfrac{F r^2}{m_1 m_2}$.

Substituting the SI units for each quantity: $F$ is in Newtons ($\mathrm{N}$), $r$ is in meters ($\mathrm{m}$), and $m$ is in kilograms ($\mathrm{kg}$).

The unit of $G$ is $\dfrac{\mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{m}^2}{\mathrm{kg} \cdot \mathrm{kg}} = \mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{m}^2 \cdot \mathrm{kg}^{-2}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{N} \mathrm{m}^2 \mathrm{~kg}^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The rms velocity of the gas molecule at $327^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is same as the rms velocity of the oxygen molecules at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. If the molecular weight of oxygen is 32 then the molecular weight of the given gas molecule is:
questions.solution:
The root mean square velocity of a gas is given by the formula $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$, where $R$ is the universal gas constant, $T$ is the absolute temperature in Kelvin, and $M$ is the molar mass of the gas.

Given that the rms velocity of the gas at $T_1 = 327^{\circ}C$ is equal to the rms velocity of oxygen at $T_2 = 27^{\circ}C$, we have:

$\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT_1}{M_1}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT_2}{M_2}}$

Squaring both sides and simplifying, we get:

$\dfrac{T_1}{M_1} = \dfrac{T_2}{M_2}$

Convert the temperatures to Kelvin:

$T_1 = 327 + 273 = 600 \text{ K}$

$T_2 = 27 + 273 = 300 \text{ K}$

The molar mass of oxygen $M_2 = 32$. Substituting the values into the equation:

$\dfrac{600}{M_1} = \dfrac{300}{32}$

$M_1 = \dfrac{600 \times 32}{300}$

$M_1 = 2 \times 32 = 64$

Answer: $64$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The total number of degrees of freedom associated with $2 \mathrm{~cm}^3$ of Nitrogen gas at normal temperature and pressure is:
[Given Avogadro number as ' N ' ]
questions.solution:
At normal temperature and pressure (NTP), the molar volume of an ideal gas is $22400 \text{ cm}^3$.

The number of moles $n$ in $2 \text{ cm}^3$ of Nitrogen gas is given by $n = \dfrac{V}{V_{m}} = \dfrac{2}{22400} = \dfrac{1}{11200}$ moles.

Nitrogen ($N_2$) is a diatomic gas. The degrees of freedom $f$ for a diatomic molecule at room temperature is $5$ (3 translational and 2 rotational).

The total number of molecules $N_{total}$ is $n \times N$, where $N$ is the Avogadro number. Thus, $N_{total} = \dfrac{N}{11200}$.

The total degrees of freedom is given by $f \times N_{total} = 5 \times \dfrac{N}{11200} = \dfrac{N}{2240}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{N}{2240}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass 10 kg is moving up on an inclined plane of $30^{\circ}$ with an acceleration $2 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$. Find the force required, if the coefficient of friction between the object and the plane surface is $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6}$, [given $g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$ ].
questions.solution:
The forces acting on the body of mass $m = 10$ kg moving up the inclined plane are the applied force $F$ (acting up the plane), the component of gravitational force $mg \sin \theta$ (acting down the plane), and the frictional force $f_k$ (acting down the plane).

The equation of motion is $F - mg \sin \theta - f_k = ma$.

The normal force $N$ exerted by the plane is $N = mg \cos \theta$.

The frictional force is $f_k = \mu N = \mu mg \cos \theta$.

Given $m = 10$ kg, $g = 10$ ms$^{-2}$, $\theta = 30^{\circ}$, $a = 2$ ms$^{-2}$, and $\mu = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6}$.

Calculating the components:
$mg \sin 30^{\circ} = 10 \times 10 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 50$ N.
$f_k = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6} \times 10 \times 10 \times \cos 30^{\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{6} \times 100 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{3 \times 100}{12} = \dfrac{300}{12} = 25$ N.

Substituting these values into the equation of motion:
$F - 50 - 25 = 10 \times 2$
$F - 75 = 20$
$F = 95$ N.

Answer: 95 N

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a particular case $X$, a certain length of insulated copper wire is bent to form double loops of equal radii. In another case Y the same copper wire is bent to form three loops of equal radii. If the same steady current is passed through the copper wire in both the cases, the ratio of magnetic field at the centre in the case X to that in case Y is:
questions.solution:
Let $L$ be the total length of the wire. In case $X$, the wire is bent into $n_1 = 2$ loops of radius $r_1$. The circumference of these loops is $2 \times (2 \pi r_1) = L$, so $r_1 = \dfrac{L}{4 \pi}$.

The magnetic field at the center of $n_1$ loops is $B_X = n_1 \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 r_1} = 2 \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 (L / 4 \pi)} = \dfrac{4 \pi \mu_0 I}{L}$.

In case $Y$, the wire is bent into $n_2 = 3$ loops of radius $r_2$. The circumference of these loops is $3 \times (2 \pi r_2) = L$, so $r_2 = \dfrac{L}{6 \pi}$.

The magnetic field at the center of $n_2$ loops is $B_Y = n_2 \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 r_2} = 3 \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 (L / 6 \pi)} = \dfrac{9 \pi \mu_0 I}{L}$.

The ratio of the magnetic fields is $\dfrac{B_X}{B_Y} = \dfrac{4 \pi \mu_0 I / L}{9 \pi \mu_0 I / L} = \dfrac{4}{9}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{4}{9}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A current carrying closed loop in the form of a right isosceles triangle XYZ is placed in a uniform magnetic field $B$ acting along $X Y$ of the loop. If the magnetic force on the $\operatorname{arm} Y Z$ is $\sqrt{2} F$, then the force on the arm $X Z$ is:
questions.solution:
The net magnetic force on a closed current-carrying loop in a uniform field is zero:
$\vec{F}_{XY} + \vec{F}_{YZ} + \vec{F}_{XZ} = 0$

Since field $B$ acts along arm $XY$, the arm $XY$ is parallel to $\vec{B}$, so $\vec{F}_{XY} = 0$.

Therefore:
$\vec{F}_{XZ} = -\vec{F}_{YZ} = -\sqrt{2}F$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A short bar magnet placed with its axis at $45^{\circ}$ with an external field of $400 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~T}$ experiences a torque of 0.024 Nm . If a solenoid of cross-sectional area $10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2$ and 500 turns replaces the short bar magnet such that they have the same magnetic moment, then the current flowing through the solenoid is:
questions.solution:
The torque $\tau$ experienced by a magnetic dipole in an external magnetic field $B$ is given by $\tau = mB \sin \theta$, where $m$ is the magnetic moment and $\theta$ is the angle between the magnetic moment and the magnetic field.

Given $\tau = 0.024 \text{ Nm}$, $B = 400 \times 10^{-4} \text{ T} = 0.04 \text{ T}$, and $\theta = 45^{\circ}$.

Substituting the values: $0.024 = m \times 0.04 \times \sin(45^{\circ})$.

$0.024 = m \times 0.04 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.

$m = \dfrac{0.024 \times \sqrt{2}}{0.04} = 0.6 \sqrt{2} \text{ Am}^2$.

The magnetic moment of a solenoid is given by $m = NIA$, where $N$ is the number of turns, $I$ is the current, and $A$ is the cross-sectional area.

Given $N = 500$ and $A = 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$.

Equating the magnetic moments: $0.6 \sqrt{2} = 500 \times I \times 10^{-4}$.

$0.6 \sqrt{2} = 0.05 \times I$.

$I = \dfrac{0.6 \sqrt{2}}{0.05} = \dfrac{60 \sqrt{2}}{5} = 12 \sqrt{2} \text{ A}$.

Answer: $12 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{~A}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A straight wire of mass 250 g and length 2.5 m carries a current of 4 A . It can be suspended in mid air by a uniform horizontal magnetic field of magnitude:
questions.solution:
The wire is suspended in mid-air, which implies that the magnetic force acting on the wire must balance the gravitational force acting on it.

The gravitational force $F_g$ acting on the wire is given by $F_g = mg$, where $m = 250 \text{ g} = 0.25 \text{ kg}$ and $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$.

$F_g = 0.25 \times 9.8 = 2.45 \text{ N}$.

The magnetic force $F_m$ on a current-carrying wire in a uniform magnetic field is given by $F_m = IlB \sin(\theta)$. Since the magnetic field is horizontal and the wire is suspended, the force is perpendicular to the wire, so $\theta = 90^{\circ}$ and $\sin(90^{\circ}) = 1$.

$F_m = IlB$.

Equating the forces, $IlB = mg$.

$B = \dfrac{mg}{Il} = \dfrac{0.25 \times 9.8}{4 \times 2.5} = \dfrac{2.45}{10} = 0.245 \text{ T}$.

Answer: 0.245 T

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal rod of susceptibility 799 is subjected to a magnetising field of $2000 \mathrm{Am}^{-1}$. The permeability of the material of the rod is: (Given $\mu_0=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{TmA}^{-1}$ )
questions.solution:
The magnetic susceptibility $\chi$ of the material is given as $799$.

The relative permeability $\mu_r$ is related to the magnetic susceptibility by the formula $\mu_r = 1 + \chi$.

Substituting the given value, $\mu_r = 1 + 799 = 800$.

The absolute permeability $\mu$ of the material is given by $\mu = \mu_0 \mu_r$.

Given $\mu_0 = 4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \text{ TmA}^{-1}$, we have $\mu = (4 \pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 800$.

Calculating the value, $\mu = 3200 \pi \times 10^{-7} \text{ TmA}^{-1} = 3.2 \pi \times 10^{-4} \text{ TmA}^{-1}$.

Answer: $3.2 \pi \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{TmA}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In to a vessel containing pure water a clean glass tube of radius $3.6 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}$ is held vertically with 12 cm of the tube above the water level. Now the capillary tube is moved down in to the water so that only 2 cm of its length is above the water surface. Angle of contact $\theta$ at this position is (given surface tension of water $=7.2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{Nm}^{-1}$ and $g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
The capillary rise $h$ in a tube of radius $r$ is given by the formula $h = \dfrac{2T \cos \theta}{r \rho g}$, where $T$ is the surface tension, $\theta$ is the angle of contact, $\rho$ is the density of water, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

First, calculate the maximum capillary rise $h_{max}$ for pure water in a glass tube, where $\theta = 0^{\circ}$ and $\cos 0^{\circ} = 1$. Given $T = 7.2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ N/m}$, $r = 3.6 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$, $\rho = 1000 \text{ kg/m}^3$, and $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$h_{max} = \dfrac{2 \times 7.2 \times 10^{-2}}{3.6 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000 \times 10} = \dfrac{14.4 \times 10^{-2}}{3.6 \times 10^0} = 4 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 4 \text{ cm}$.

When the tube is pushed down such that only $2 \text{ cm}$ is above the water surface, the water cannot rise higher than the top of the tube. The water will rise to the top of the tube, and the meniscus will adjust its curvature to satisfy the equilibrium condition $h' = \dfrac{2T \cos \theta}{r \rho g}$, where $h' = 2 \text{ cm}$.

Substituting the values: $2 \times 10^{-2} = \dfrac{2 \times 7.2 \times 10^{-2} \cos \theta}{3.6 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000 \times 10}$.

$2 \times 10^{-2} = \dfrac{14.4 \times 10^{-2} \cos \theta}{3.6} = 4 \times 10^{-2} \cos \theta$.

Therefore, $\cos \theta = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-2}}{4 \times 10^{-2}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

This gives $\theta = 60^{\circ}$.

Answer: $\theta=60^{\circ}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Select the correct statement from the following:
options: The bulk modulus of an ideal liquid is zero
Rubber is more elastic than steel
Shear modulus of an ideal liquid is infinite
The bulk modulus of a perfect rigid body is infinite
questions.solution:
The bulk modulus $B$ is defined as $B = -V \dfrac{dP}{dV}$. For a perfectly rigid body, the change in volume $dV$ is zero for any applied pressure $dP$. Thus, $B = -V \dfrac{dP}{0} = \infty$.

Regarding other options: The bulk modulus of an ideal liquid is finite and positive, not zero. Steel is more elastic than rubber because the Young's modulus of steel is much higher than that of rubber, meaning it requires more stress to produce the same strain. The shear modulus of an ideal liquid is zero because it cannot sustain any shear stress.

Answer: The bulk modulus of a perfect rigid body is infinite

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Select the graph which represents the motion of a particle along a straight line with uniform acceleration.
questions.solution:
For a particle moving in a straight line with uniform acceleration $a$, the velocity $v$ at time $t$ is given by the equation $v = u + at$, where $u$ is the initial velocity.

If the particle starts from rest ($u = 0$), the equation becomes $v = at$. This represents a linear relationship between velocity and time, which is a straight line passing through the origin with a slope equal to the acceleration $a$.

Among the given options, the third graph shows a velocity-time graph that is a straight line passing through the origin, which corresponds to motion with uniform acceleration starting from rest.

Answer:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A boy is running along a straight horizontal road with a constant speed $5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. While running he throws a stone with a velocity $30 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$ at an angle $60^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. Then the time of flight of the stone is: (Given $g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$ )
questions.solution:
The velocity of the stone is given with respect to the boy. Let the velocity of the boy be $\vec{v}_b = 5 \hat{i} \text{ ms}^{-1}$. The velocity of the stone with respect to the boy is $\vec{v}_{s/b} = 30 \cos 60^{\circ} \hat{i} + 30 \sin 60^{\circ} \hat{j} \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

The velocity of the stone with respect to the ground is $\vec{v}_s = \vec{v}_{s/b} + \vec{v}_b = (30 \times 0.5 + 5) \hat{i} + (30 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \hat{j} \text{ ms}^{-1} = 20 \hat{i} + 15\sqrt{3} \hat{j} \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

The time of flight $T$ for a projectile depends only on the vertical component of the initial velocity $u_y$ and the acceleration due to gravity $g$.

$T = \dfrac{2 u_y}{g} = \dfrac{2 \times 15\sqrt{3}}{10} = \dfrac{30\sqrt{3}}{10} = 3\sqrt{3} \text{ s}$.

Answer: $3 \sqrt{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When ${ }^{10} \mathrm{~B}_5$ nuclei are bombarded by neutrons, one of the resultant nuclei is ${ }^7 \mathrm{Li}_3$. Then the emitted particle will be:
questions.solution:
The nuclear reaction can be represented as follows:

${}^{10}_{5}\text{B} + {}^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow {}^{7}_{3}\text{Li} + {}^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$

Applying the law of conservation of mass number (A):

$10 + 1 = 7 + A \Rightarrow 11 = 7 + A \Rightarrow A = 4$

Applying the law of conservation of atomic number (Z):

$5 + 0 = 3 + Z \Rightarrow 5 = 3 + Z \Rightarrow Z = 2$

The particle with mass number 4 and atomic number 2 is the alpha particle (${}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ or $\alpha$).

Answer: Alpha particle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Radium having mass number 200 and binding energy per nucleon 5.6 MeV , splits into two fragments Cadmium of mass number 112 and Hassium of mass number 108. If the binding energy per nucleon for Cadmium and Hassium is approximately 8.0 MeV , then the energy Q released per fission will be:
questions.solution:
The total binding energy of the parent nucleus (Radium) is given by the product of its mass number and its binding energy per nucleon.

Total binding energy of Radium = $200 \times 5.6 \text{ MeV} = 1120 \text{ MeV}$.

The total binding energy of the daughter nuclei (Cadmium and Hassium) is the sum of their individual binding energies.

Total binding energy of fragments = $(112 \times 8.0 \text{ MeV}) + (108 \times 8.0 \text{ MeV}) = (112 + 108) \times 8.0 \text{ MeV} = 220 \times 8.0 \text{ MeV} = 1760 \text{ MeV}$.

The energy released $Q$ in the fission process is the difference between the total binding energy of the products and the total binding energy of the reactant.

$Q = 1760 \text{ MeV} - 1120 \text{ MeV} = 640 \text{ MeV}$.

Answer: 640 MeV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the mass numbers of two nuclei are in the ratio \(5: 2\) and their diameters are in ratio \(2: 6\), Then their nuclear densities will be in the ratio
questions.solution:
The nuclear radius $R$ is related to the mass number $A$ by the formula $R = R_{0} A^{1/3}$, where $R_{0}$ is a constant. The diameter $D$ is proportional to the radius, so $D \propto A^{1/3}$.

The nuclear density $\rho$ is defined as the ratio of the mass of the nucleus to its volume. The mass of a nucleus is approximately $M = A \times m_{p}$, where $m_{p}$ is the mass of a nucleon. The volume of a nucleus is $V = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^{3} = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi (R_{0} A^{1/3})^{3} = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R_{0}^{3} A$.

The nuclear density is $\rho = \dfrac{M}{V} = \dfrac{A m_{p}}{\dfrac{4}{3} \pi R_{0}^{3} A} = \dfrac{m_{p}}{\dfrac{4}{3} \pi R_{0}^{3}}$.

Since $m_{p}$, $R_{0}$, and $\pi$ are constants, the nuclear density $\rho$ is independent of the mass number $A$. Therefore, the ratio of the nuclear densities of any two nuclei is always $1: 1$.

Answer: \(1: 1\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Select the correct statement from the following:
options: Nuclear force is the weakest force in nature
Nuclear force is a non central force
Nuclear force depends on the charge of the nucleons
Nuclear force is a long range force
questions.solution:
Nuclear forces are the strongest forces in nature, acting between nucleons within the nucleus. They are short-range forces, effective only up to distances of the order of $10^{-15}$ m (femtometers).

Nuclear forces are charge-independent, meaning they act equally between proton-proton, neutron-neutron, and proton-neutron pairs, provided the distance is the same.

Nuclear forces are non-central forces, as they do not act only along the line joining the centers of the two nucleons; they depend on the spin and orientation of the nucleons.

Answer: Nuclear force is a non central force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A wire of negligible mass having uniform area of cross section 'A' and young modulus ' Y ' is used to suspend a point mass ' m '. The point mass executes simple harmonic motion in a vertical plane with a period ' T ', then the length of the wire is :
questions.solution:
The wire acts as a spring with a spring constant $k$ given by the formula $k = \dfrac{YA}{L}$, where $Y$ is the Young modulus, $A$ is the area of cross-section, and $L$ is the length of the wire.

The time period $T$ of a mass $m$ executing simple harmonic motion attached to a spring of constant $k$ is given by $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$.

Squaring both sides of the equation, we get $T^2 = 4\pi^2 \dfrac{m}{k}$.

Substituting the expression for $k$ into the equation for $T^2$, we have $T^2 = 4\pi^2 \dfrac{m}{(YA/L)}$.

Rearranging the equation to solve for $L$, we get $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2 mL}{YA}$.

Therefore, $L = \dfrac{T^2 YA}{4\pi^2 m}$.

Answer: $L=\dfrac{T^2 Y A}{4 \pi^2 m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A plano-convex lens made of refractive index 1.5 and having radius of curvature $\mathrm{R}=4 \mathrm{~cm}$ fits exactly into a planoconcave lens made of refractive index 1.3 and having the same radius of curvature $R=4 \mathrm{~cm}$ such that their plane surfaces are parallel to each other. The focal length of the combination is:
questions.solution:
For the plano-convex lens ($\mu_1 = 1.5$), $R_1 = \infty$, $R_2 = -4$ cm:

$\dfrac{1}{f_1} = (1.5 - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{\infty} - \dfrac{1}{-4}\right) = \dfrac{0.5}{4}$ cm$^{-1}$

For the plano-concave lens ($\mu_2 = 1.3$), $R_1 = -4$ cm, $R_2 = \infty$:

$\dfrac{1}{f_2} = (1.3 - 1)\left(\dfrac{1}{-4} - 0\right) = -\dfrac{0.3}{4}$ cm$^{-1}$

$\dfrac{1}{F} = \dfrac{0.5}{4} - \dfrac{0.3}{4} = \dfrac{0.2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{20}$ cm$^{-1}$

$F = 20$ cm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An object of height $h$ is placed midway between $f$ and $2 f$ in front of a biconvex lens. A real inverted image is captured on a screen placed a little beyond $2 f$ on the other side of the lens. If the whole arrangement is immersed in water without disturbing the object, lens and the screen positions, then the new image formed will be
options: Magnified real inverted image on the same side of the lens where the object is placed
Diminished real inverted image on the other side of the lens between $f$ and $2 f$
Magnified real inverted image on the other side of the lens beyond $2 f$
Magnified virtual erect image on the same side of the lens where the object is placed
questions.solution:
The focal length of a lens in a medium of refractive index $n_m$ is given by the lens maker formula: $\dfrac{1}{f_m} = (\dfrac{n_l}{n_m} - 1)(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2})$.

Initially, in air ($n_m = 1$), the focal length is $f$. When immersed in water ($n_m = 1.33$), the refractive index ratio $\dfrac{n_l}{n_m}$ decreases, which increases the focal length $f_m$ of the lens. Let the new focal length be $f' \gt f$.

The object is placed at a distance $u$ such that $f \lt u \lt 2f$. Since the lens is now in water, the new focal length $f'$ satisfies $f' \gt f$. The object position $u$ now satisfies $u \lt f'$.

When an object is placed within the focal length of a convex lens ($u \lt f'$), the lens acts as a simple magnifier. The image formed is virtual, erect, and magnified, and it is formed on the same side of the lens as the object.

Since the screen is fixed at the original position beyond $2f$, and the image is now virtual and formed on the same side as the object, no real image will be captured on the screen.

Answer: Magnified virtual erect image on the same side of the lens where the object is placed

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A beam of incident parallel light falls on a diverging lens of focal length 20 cm in magnitude. If a converging lens of focal length 15 cm in magnitude is placed at a distance of 10 cm to the right of the diverging lens on the other side, then, the final image formed is:
options: Virtual and is at a distance of 40 cm to the right of the diverging lens.
Real and is at a distance of 40 cm to the right of the converging lens.
Real and is at a distance of 30 cm to the right of the converging lens.
Virtual and is at a distance of 30 cm to the right of the converging lens.
questions.solution:
For the diverging lens, the focal length $f_1 = -20$ cm. Since the incident light is parallel, the rays appear to diverge from the focus of the diverging lens located at $20$ cm to the left of the lens. The image formed by the first lens acts as the object for the second lens.

The position of this virtual object for the second lens is $10$ cm (distance between lenses) $+ 20$ cm (focal length of first lens) $= 30$ cm to the left of the converging lens. Thus, $u_2 = -30$ cm.

For the converging lens, the focal length $f_2 = +15$ cm. Using the lens formula $\dfrac{1}{v_2} - \dfrac{1}{u_2} = \dfrac{1}{f_2}$, we have $\dfrac{1}{v_2} - \dfrac{1}{-30} = \dfrac{1}{15}$.

Solving for $v_2$: $\dfrac{1}{v_2} = \dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{2-1}{30} = \dfrac{1}{30}$.

Therefore, $v_2 = +30$ cm. The positive sign indicates that the image is real and formed at a distance of $30$ cm to the right of the converging lens.

Answer: Real and is at a distance of 30 cm to the right of the converging lens.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In the normal adjustment of an astronomical telescope, the objective and eyepiece are 36 cm apart. If the magnifying power of the telescope is 8, find the focal lengths of the objective and eyepiece.
questions.solution:

Given $M = 8$, we have $\dfrac{f_o}{f_e} = 8$, which implies $f_o = 8f_e$.

Substituting $f_o = 8f_e$ into the first equation: $8f_e + f_e = 36$.

$9f_e = 36 \Rightarrow f_e = 4 \text{ cm}$.

Then $f_o = 8 \times 4 = 32 \text{ cm}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{o}}=32 \mathrm{~cm}, \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{e}}=4 \mathrm{~cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Applying a constant torque the speed of a flywheel is increased from 1800 rpm to 2400 rpm in 10 seconds. The number of revolutions made by the flywheel during this time is:
questions.solution:
Initial angular velocity $\omega_0 = 1800 \text{ rpm} = \dfrac{1800 \times 2\pi}{60} \text{ rad/s} = 60\pi \text{ rad/s}$.

Final angular velocity $\omega = 2400 \text{ rpm} = \dfrac{2400 \times 2\pi}{60} \text{ rad/s} = 80\pi \text{ rad/s}$.

Time interval $t = 10 \text{ s}$.

Assuming constant angular acceleration $\alpha$, the average angular velocity is $\omega_{avg} = \dfrac{\omega_0 + \omega}{2} = \dfrac{60\pi + 80\pi}{2} = 70\pi \text{ rad/s}$.

Total angular displacement $\theta = \omega_{avg} \times t = 70\pi \times 10 = 700\pi \text{ radians}$.

The number of revolutions $N$ is given by $\theta = N \times 2\pi$.

$N = \dfrac{\theta}{2\pi} = \dfrac{700\pi}{2\pi} = 350$.

Answer: $350$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A point marked on a ring of radius 2 cm is in contact with a horizontal plane. Now the ring is rolled forward half a revolution along the positive X - direction. Then the angle made by the displacement vector of the point with the X - axis is:
questions.solution:
Let the radius of the ring be $R = 2$ cm. Initially, the point is at the origin $(0, 0)$ in contact with the horizontal plane (X-axis).

The ring rolls forward by half a revolution. The distance moved by the center of the ring is $d = R \times \theta_{rot} = R \times \pi = 2\pi$.

After half a revolution, the center of the ring is at $(2\pi, 2)$. The point, which was initially at the bottom, is now at the top of the ring. The coordinates of the point after half a revolution are $(2\pi, 2R) = (2\pi, 4)$.

The displacement vector $\vec{S}$ of the point from its initial position $(0, 0)$ to its final position $(2\pi, 4)$ is $\vec{S} = (2\pi - 0)\hat{i} + (4 - 0)\hat{j} = 2\pi\hat{i} + 4\hat{j}$.

The angle $\theta$ made by the displacement vector with the X-axis is given by $\tan \theta = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{4}{2\pi} = \dfrac{2}{\pi}$.

Therefore, $\theta = \tan ^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)$.

Answer: $\theta=\tan ^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: What is the dc component of the output voltage if a sinusoidal signal of 33 V peak voltage is the input of a half wave diode rectifier circuit?
questions.solution:
For a half-wave rectifier, the output voltage is a rectified sine wave. The dc component or the average value of the output voltage $V_{dc}$ is given by the formula $V_{dc} = \dfrac{V_m}{\pi}$, where $V_m$ is the peak voltage of the input sinusoidal signal.

Given $V_m = 33$ V, we substitute this value into the formula:

$V_{dc} = \dfrac{33}{\pi}$

Using the approximation $\pi \approx 3.14159$:

$V_{dc} \approx \dfrac{33}{3.14159} \approx 10.504$ V.

Rounding to the nearest value provided in the options, we get $10.5$ V.

Answer: 10.5 V

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: An intrinsic semiconductor has equal concentrations of hole and electron which is equal to $4 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m}^{-3}$. During its conversion to extrinsic semiconductor, concentration of hole increases to $8 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~m}^{-3}$. The new electron concentration is:
questions.solution:
For an intrinsic semiconductor, the intrinsic carrier concentration $n_i$ is given by $n_i = n_e = n_h = 4 \times 10^8 \text{ m}^{-3}$.

The law of mass action for semiconductors states that the product of electron concentration $n_e$ and hole concentration $n_h$ in an extrinsic semiconductor remains constant and equal to the square of the intrinsic carrier concentration:

$n_e \times n_h = n_i^2$

Given the new hole concentration $n_h = 8 \times 10^{10} \text{ m}^{-3}$, we substitute the values into the equation:

$n_e \times (8 \times 10^{10}) = (4 \times 10^8)^2$

$n_e \times (8 \times 10^{10}) = 16 \times 10^{16}$

$n_e = \dfrac{16 \times 10^{16}}{8 \times 10^{10}}$

$n_e = 2 \times 10^6 \text{ m}^{-3}$

Answer: $2 \times 10^6 \mathrm{~m}^{-3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The zener voltage in the circuit shown is $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{Z}}=20 \mathrm{~V}$. The load resistance $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{L}}=5 \mathrm{k} \Omega$ and the resistance $\mathrm{R} \mathrm{s}=10 \mathrm{k} \Omega$. If the input voltage is $\mathrm{V} \mathrm{s}=100 \mathrm{~V}$, then the current through the zener diode in milliampere is:
questions.solution:
The circuit is a Zener diode voltage regulator. The Zener diode is connected in parallel with the load resistor $R_L$.

Given values:
$V_S = 100 \text{ V}$
$R_S = 10 \text{ k}\Omega = 10000 \Omega$
$R_L = 5 \text{ k}\Omega = 5000 \Omega$
$V_Z = 20 \text{ V}$

Since the Zener diode is in parallel with the load resistor $R_L$, the voltage across the load resistor $V_L$ is equal to the Zener voltage $V_Z$.
$V_L = V_Z = 20 \text{ V}$

The total current $I$ flowing through the series resistor $R_S$ is given by:
$I = \dfrac{V_S - V_Z}{R_S} = \dfrac{100 - 20}{10000} = \dfrac{80}{10000} = 8 \times 10^{-3} \text{ A} = 8 \text{ mA}$

The current flowing through the load resistor $I_L$ is:
$I_L = \dfrac{V_L}{R_L} = \dfrac{20}{5000} = 4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ A} = 4 \text{ mA}$

Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law at the node connecting $R_S$, the Zener diode, and $R_L$, the current through the Zener diode $I_Z$ is:
$I_Z = I - I_L = 8 \text{ mA} - 4 \text{ mA} = 4 \text{ mA}$

Answer: $4$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The rate of heat conduction in the given two metal rods having the same length is found to be the same when the temperature difference between the ends is kept $30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ If the area of cross section of the first rod is $8 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}^2$ then what will be area of cross section of the second rod? [ Given that the ratio of the thermal conductivity of the first rod to that of the second rod is $1: 4$ ]
questions.solution:
The rate of heat conduction $H$ through a rod is given by the formula $H = \dfrac{KA \Delta T}{L}$, where $K$ is the thermal conductivity, $A$ is the area of cross-section, $\Delta T$ is the temperature difference, and $L$ is the length of the rod.

Given that the rate of heat conduction is the same for both rods, we have $H_1 = H_2$. Substituting the formula for both rods:

$\dfrac{K_1 A_1 \Delta T_1}{L_1} = \dfrac{K_2 A_2 \Delta T_2}{L_2}$

Since the lengths $L_1 = L_2$ and the temperature differences $\Delta T_1 = \Delta T_2 = 30^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ are the same, the equation simplifies to:

$K_1 A_1 = K_2 A_2$

Rearranging to solve for $A_2$:

$A_2 = A_1 \times \left( \dfrac{K_1}{K_2} \right)$

Given $A_1 = 8 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}^2$ and the ratio $\dfrac{K_1}{K_2} = \dfrac{1}{4}$, we substitute these values:

$A_2 = (8 \times 10^{-2}) \times \left( \dfrac{1}{4} \right) = 2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}^2$

Answer: $2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A given volume of gas at NTP is allowed to expand 6 times of its original volume, first under isothermal condition and then under adiabatic condition. Which of the given statement is correct?
[Given $\dfrac{C_p}{C_v}=\gamma=1.4$ ]
options: The final pressure after the adiabatic expansion is less than the final pressure after the isothermal expansion.
Pressure remains same in both adiabatic and isothermal expansion
The final temperature after the adiabatic expansion is 1.4 times less than the final temperature after the isothermal expansion.
The final pressure after the adiabatic expansion is 1.4 times greater than the final pressure after the isothermal expansion.
questions.solution:
Let the initial pressure be $P_0$, initial volume be $V_0$, and initial temperature be $T_0$. The gas expands to a final volume $V_f = 6V_0$.

For isothermal expansion, the final pressure $P_{iso}$ is given by $P_0 V_0 = P_{iso} (6V_0)$, which gives $P_{iso} = \dfrac{P_0}{6}$.

For adiabatic expansion, the final pressure $P_{adia}$ is given by $P_0 V_0^{\gamma} = P_{adia} (6V_0)^{\gamma}$, which gives $P_{adia} = P_0 \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^{\gamma}$.

Given $\gamma = 1.4$, we have $P_{adia} = P_0 \left( \dfrac{1}{6} \right)^{1.4}$.

Comparing $P_{iso} = P_0 (6)^{-1}$ and $P_{adia} = P_0 (6)^{-1.4}$, since $6^{1.4} \gt 6^1$, it follows that $\dfrac{1}{6^{1.4}} \lt \dfrac{1}{6^1}$.

Therefore, $P_{adia} \lt P_{iso}$. The final pressure after adiabatic expansion is less than the final pressure after isothermal expansion.

Answer: The final pressure after the adiabatic expansion is less than the final pressure after the isothermal expansion.

questions.solution:
The dimensional formula for Stress is $\dfrac{\text{Force}}{\text{Area}} = \dfrac{[M^1 L^1 T^{-2}]}{[L^2]} = [M^1 L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

The dimensional formula for Pressure is $\dfrac{\text{Force}}{\text{Area}} = \dfrac{[M^1 L^1 T^{-2}]}{[L^2]} = [M^1 L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

Since both Stress and Pressure have the same dimensional formula $[M^1 L^{-1} T^{-2}]$, they are the correct pair.

Answer: Stress and Pressure

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Young's double slit experiment is first done in air and then in a medium of refractive index $\mu$. If the 8th dark fringe in the medium lies where the 4th bright fringe is in air, then the value of $\mu$ is:
questions.solution:
Position of 4th bright fringe in air: $y_{4,air} = 4\dfrac{\lambda D}{d}$

In medium of refractive index $\mu$, wavelength becomes $\lambda' = \dfrac{\lambda}{\mu}$. Position of 8th dark fringe in medium:
$y_{8,medium} = (8 - 0.5)\dfrac{\lambda' D}{d} = \dfrac{7.5\lambda D}{\mu d}$

Equating the two positions:
$\dfrac{7.5\lambda D}{\mu d} = \dfrac{4\lambda D}{d}$

$\mu = \dfrac{7.5}{4} = 1.875$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The wavelength of a monochromatic light which is used in single slit diffraction is 800 nm . The width of the single slit for which the first minimum appears at $\theta=45^{\circ}$ on the screen will be:
questions.solution:
The condition for the first minimum in single slit diffraction is given by the formula $a \sin \theta = n \lambda$, where $a$ is the width of the slit, $\theta$ is the angle of diffraction, $n$ is the order of the minimum, and $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the light.

Given values are $\lambda = 800 \text{ nm} = 800 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$ and $\theta = 45^{\circ}$. For the first minimum, $n = 1$.

Substituting these values into the formula:

$a \sin 45^{\circ} = 1 \times 800 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$

$a \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 800 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$

$a = 800 \times \sqrt{2} \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$

Using $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$:

$a = 800 \times 1.414 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$

$a = 1131.2 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$

$a = 1.1312 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m} = 1.13 \mu \text{m}$

Answer: $1.13 \mu \mathrm{~m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The interference pattern is obtained with two coherent light sources of intensity ratio $9: 1$.
The ratio of $\dfrac{I_{\text {MAX }}+I_{\text {MIN }}}{I_{\text {MAX }}-I_{\text {MIN }}}$ is $\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}$. The values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are:
questions.solution:
Let the intensities of the two coherent sources be $I_1$ and $I_2$. Given the ratio $I_1 : I_2 = 9 : 1$, we can write $I_1 = 9k$ and $I_2 = k$ for some constant $k$.

The amplitudes $a_1$ and $a_2$ are proportional to the square root of the intensities, so $a_1 = \sqrt{9k} = 3\sqrt{k}$ and $a_2 = \sqrt{k}$.

The maximum intensity $I_{\text{MAX}}$ and minimum intensity $I_{\text{MIN}}$ in an interference pattern are given by $I_{\text{MAX}} = (\sqrt{I_1} + \sqrt{I_2})^2$ and $I_{\text{MIN}} = (\sqrt{I_1} - \sqrt{I_2})^2$.

Substituting the values, $I_{\text{MAX}} = (3\sqrt{k} + \sqrt{k})^2 = (4\sqrt{k})^2 = 16k$ and $I_{\text{MIN}} = (3\sqrt{k} - \sqrt{k})^2 = (2\sqrt{k})^2 = 4k$.

The required ratio is $\dfrac{I_{\text{MAX}} + I_{\text{MIN}}}{I_{\text{MAX}} - I_{\text{MIN}}} = \dfrac{16k + 4k}{16k - 4k} = \dfrac{20k}{12k} = \dfrac{20}{12} = \dfrac{5}{3}$.

Comparing this with $\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}$, we get $\alpha = 5$ and $\beta = 3$.

Answer: 5 and 3

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The fundamental frequency of sound produced in an open pipe of length $\mathrm{L}_1$ is same as the frequency of the $3^{\text {rd }}$ harmonic of the sound produced in the closed pipe of length $\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{2}}$ Then the ratio of $\dfrac{\boldsymbol{L}_{\mathrm{1}}}{\boldsymbol{L}_{\mathrm{2}}}$ is :
questions.solution:
The fundamental frequency of an open pipe of length $L_1$ is given by $f_1 = \dfrac{v}{2L_1}$, where $v$ is the speed of sound.

The frequencies of a closed pipe of length $L_2$ are given by $f_n = \dfrac{nv}{4L_2}$, where $n$ is an odd integer ($n = 1, 3, 5, \dots$). The $3^{rd}$ harmonic of a closed pipe corresponds to the $3^{rd}$ overtone frequency, which is the $5^{th}$ harmonic ($n=5$). However, in many contexts, the $3^{rd}$ harmonic of a closed pipe is simply the $3^{rd}$ allowed frequency, which corresponds to $n=5$. Let us verify the standard terminology: the harmonics of a closed pipe are $1^{st}$ ($n=1$), $3^{rd}$ ($n=3$), $5^{th}$ ($n=5$). Thus, the $3^{rd}$ harmonic of the closed pipe is $f_3 = \dfrac{3v}{4L_2}$.

Equating the fundamental frequency of the open pipe to the $3^{rd}$ harmonic of the closed pipe:

$\dfrac{v}{2L_1} = \dfrac{3v}{4L_2}$

Simplifying the equation:

$\dfrac{1}{2L_1} = \dfrac{3}{4L_2}$

$\dfrac{L_1}{L_2} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Answer: $\dfrac{L_1}{L_2}=\dfrac{2}{3}$
